What Is Instagram Really Showing Me?

Instagram thinks I want a job — and some entertainment

I logged 40 Instagram ads over a short observation period. The results were surprising: nearly half of all ads fell into just two categories — Entertainment (games, streaming, events) dominated with 16 ads, followed closely by hiring ads with 13. Categories like Travel and student allowance barely appeared. This suggests Instagram’s algorithm has built a very specific profile of me: a young person who likes entertainment and might be looking for work — not entirely wrong, but the dominance of these two categories raises questions about how narrow the targeting really is.

Bar chart showing ad category frequency. Entertainment leads with 16 ads, hiring second with 13, while Travel, student allowance, Tech and Health each have 3 or fewer.

The longer I scroll, the less relevant the ads get

Each dot represents one ad, plotted in the order I observed it. The downward trend line tells a clear story: ads shown earlier in my scrolling session felt more relevant to my interests, while later ads increasingly scored 1 out of 5. This could suggest that Instagram’s algorithm “runs out” of well-targeted ads fairly quickly, falling back on generic content the longer a session goes on.

Scatter plot of relevance score (1 to 5) against observation order (1 to 40), with a downward-sloping trend line showing relevance decreasing over time. Most points cluster at score 1.

Not all ads are created equal — likes reveal the difference

Hiring ads spread widely across like counts, reflecting how varied job postings are in engagement. Student allowance ads, though few in number, clustered at surprisingly high like counts — suggesting these posts resonated strongly with audiences. Health & Fitness ads, by contrast, concentrated at very low like counts despite appearing frequently. Entertainment ads sat in the middle range.

Density plot showing distribution of log-transformed like counts per ad category. Student allowance peaks at high like counts around 7.5, hiring spreads broadly, and Health and Fitness concentrates near zero.

Reels go harder — Photo posts play it safe

Photo post ads leaned heavily toward Serious / informative tone, with very little urgency or humour. Reels, on the other hand, used a noticeably higher proportion of Urgent / promotional tone — the “50% off, limited time!” energy — alongside more Neutral content. Both formats used Aspirational and Funny tones sparingly. This makes intuitive sense: video is a more immersive format that lends itself to high-pressure sales tactics, while static images tend to inform rather than push.

Stacked proportional bar chart comparing ad tone between Photo post and Reels. Reels show more Urgent and Neutral tone, Photo posts lean more Serious and informative.
